title: Units and equations
subtitle: Converting units, standard form and rearranging the equations

types.name: Converting lengths, masses and times to SI units
types.method: Every equation on the sheet expects metres, kilograms and seconds, so convert before you substitute. Going from a small unit to a larger one (mm to m, g to kg) divides; going the other way multiplies. For areas and volumes, square or cube the length conversion: 1 m² is 100 × 100 cm² and 1 m³ is 100 × 100 × 100 cm³.
commonErrors: Multiplying when you should divide (120 cm is 1.2 m, not 12 000 m)
Converting hours to seconds by multiplying by 60 only once
Dividing cm² by 100 instead of by 10 000
Dividing cm³ by 100 or 1000 instead of by 1 000 000

worked.question: A bolt is 35 mm long. Convert this length to metres.
steps: Known: length = 35 mm. Unknown: length in m.
There are 1000 mm in 1 m, so divide by 1000.
Length = 0.035 m

practice.question: A desk is 120 cm wide. Convert this width to metres.
practice.hint: There are 100 cm in 1 m, so divide by 100.

practice.question: A packet of rice has a mass of 750 g. Convert this mass to kilograms.
practice.hint: There are 1000 g in 1 kg, so divide by 1000.

practice.question: A lorry carries 3.2 tonnes of gravel. 1 tonne = 1000 kg. Convert this mass to kilograms.
practice.hint: A tonne is bigger than a kilogram, so the number of kilograms must be bigger: multiply by 1000.

practice.question: A film lasts 2.5 hours. Convert this time to seconds.
practice.hint: Change hours to minutes first (× 60), then minutes to seconds (× 60 again).

practice.question: The front cover of a book has an area of 450 cm². Convert this area to m².
practice.hint: 1 m² is 100 cm × 100 cm = 10 000 cm², so divide by 10 000.

practice.question: A kettle holds 1500 cm³ of water. Convert this volume to m³.
practice.hint: 1 m³ is 100 cm × 100 cm × 100 cm = 1 000 000 cm³, so divide by 1 000 000.

types.name: Using prefixes: kilo, mega, giga, milli, micro, nano
types.method: A prefix in front of a unit is a multiplier. Kilo (k) means × 1000, mega (M) × 1 000 000 and giga (G) × 1 000 000 000. Milli (m) means ÷ 1000, micro (μ) ÷ 1 000 000 and nano (n) ÷ 1 000 000 000. Strip the prefix, apply the multiplier, and the value is in the base unit ready for the equation.
commonErrors: Mixing up milli (÷ 1000) and mega (× 1 000 000)
Treating a small prefix as a multiply: 20 mA is 0.02 A, not 20 000 A
Losing a zero in micro or nano: count the zeros, three per step
Leaving the prefix in and getting an answer 1000 times too big or too small

worked.question: A kettle transfers 540 kJ of energy to the water. Convert this energy to joules.
steps: Known: energy = 540 kJ. Unknown: energy in J.
kilo means × 1000.
Energy = 540 000 J

practice.question: The current through an LED is 20 mA. Convert this current to amps.
practice.hint: milli means ÷ 1000.

practice.question: A power station has an output of 1.8 GW. Convert this power to watts.
practice.hint: giga means × 1 000 000 000 (nine zeros).

practice.question: A wind turbine generates 2.5 MW on a windy day. Convert this power to watts.
practice.hint: mega means × 1 000 000 (six zeros).

practice.question: A resistor in a radio is labelled 4.7 kΩ. Convert this resistance to ohms.
practice.hint: kilo means × 1000, whatever the unit.

practice.question: A camera flash lasts 250 μs. Convert this time to seconds.
practice.hint: micro means ÷ 1 000 000 (six zeros).

practice.question: Red light has a wavelength of 650 nm. Convert this wavelength to metres.
practice.hint: nano means ÷ 1 000 000 000 (nine zeros).

types.name: Converting compound units: km/h, g/cm³ and kWh
types.method: A compound unit is two units combined, so convert each part in turn. For km/h to m/s, change the kilometres to metres (× 1000) and the hours to seconds (÷ 3600). For g/cm³ to kg/m³, change grams to kilograms (÷ 1000) and cm³ to m³ (÷ 1 000 000), which comes out as × 1000 overall. A kilowatt-hour is 1000 W for 3600 s, so 1 kWh = 3 600 000 J.
commonErrors: Converting the distance but forgetting the time (or the other way round)
Dividing by 3600 when going from m/s to km/h instead of multiplying
Using 1000 cm³ in a m³ instead of 1 000 000
Taking 1 kWh to be 1000 J or 3600 J

worked.question: A car travels at 90 km/h. Convert this speed to m/s.
steps: Known: speed = 90 km/h. Unknown: speed in m/s.
90 km in 1 hour is 90 × 1000 = 90 000 m in 3600 s.
Speed = 25 m/s

practice.question: A train travels at 108 km/h. Convert this speed to m/s.
practice.hint: Change km to m (× 1000) and hours to seconds (÷ 3600).

practice.question: A television uses 1.5 kWh of energy in a day. 1 kWh = 3 600 000 J. Convert this energy to joules.
practice.hint: Multiply the number of kWh by 3 600 000.

practice.question: A cyclist rides at 12 m/s. Convert this speed to km/h.
practice.hint: Work out how many metres are covered in one hour (3600 s), then change to km.
walkthrough: In 1 hour the cyclist covers 12 × 3600 = 43 200 m.

practice.question: Aluminium has a density of 2.7 g/cm³. Convert this density to kg/m³.
practice.hint: Change the grams to kilograms (÷ 1000) and the cm³ to m³ (÷ 1 000 000); a division in the bottom turns into a multiplication.

practice.question: A snail moves 15 cm in one minute. Calculate its speed in m/s.
practice.hint: Change 15 cm to metres and 1 minute to seconds before dividing.

practice.question: A bath tap delivers 12 litres of water per minute. 1 litre = 1000 cm³. Calculate the flow rate in m³/s.
practice.hint: Change 12 litres to cm³, then to m³ (÷ 1 000 000), then divide by 60 s.

types.name: Standard form for very large and very small values
equations: × 10ⁿ moves the decimal point n places to the right
× 10⁻ⁿ moves the decimal point n places to the left
types.method: Standard form writes a number as a × 10ⁿ with a between 1 and 10. A positive power moves the decimal point to the right (a big number); a negative power moves it to the left (a small number). To write an ordinary number in standard form, count how many places the decimal point moves to leave one non-zero digit in front of it. Where a question asks for n, give the power alone; otherwise give the ordinary number.
commonErrors: Counting the zeros instead of the places the decimal point moves (2 500 000 is 2.5 × 10⁶, not 10⁵)
Dropping the minus sign on the power for a small number
Writing 25 × 10⁵ instead of 2.5 × 10⁶ (the front number must be less than 10)
Adding powers when you should be multiplying the front numbers too

worked.question: A radio station broadcasts at a frequency of 9.8 × 10⁷ Hz. Write this frequency as an ordinary number.
steps: Known: frequency = 9.8 × 10⁷ Hz. Unknown: the ordinary number.
The power is +7, so move the decimal point 7 places to the right.
9.8 → 98 000 000 (one place uses the 8, then six zeros)
Frequency = 98 000 000 Hz

practice.question: A microwave oven uses waves of wavelength 1.2 × 10⁻² m. Write this wavelength as an ordinary number.
practice.hint: A negative power moves the decimal point to the left: 2 places here.
walkthrough: Power is −2, so move the decimal point 2 places to the left.

practice.question: The radius of the Earth is 6.4 × 10⁶ m. Write this distance as an ordinary number.
practice.hint: A positive power moves the decimal point to the right: 6 places here.
walkthrough: Power is +6, so move the decimal point 6 places to the right.
6.4 → 6 400 000 (one place uses the 4, then five zeros)

practice.question: An ultrasound scanner uses a frequency of 2 500 000 Hz. In standard form this is 2.5 × 10ⁿ Hz. State the value of n.
practice.hint: Count how many places the decimal point moves from the end of 2 500 000 to sit after the 2.
walkthrough: Put the decimal point after the first digit: 2.5
From 2 500 000. to 2.5 the point moves 6 places to the left.

practice.question: Blue light has a wavelength of 0.000 000 45 m. In standard form this is 4.5 × 10ⁿ m. State the value of n.
practice.hint: The number is smaller than 1, so n is negative; count the places the point moves to the right to sit after the 4.
walkthrough: Put the decimal point after the first non-zero digit: 4.5
From 0.000 000 45 to 4.5 the point moves 7 places to the right.
A small number needs a negative power: 4.5 × 10⁻⁷

practice.question: A laser pulse lasts 2 × 10⁻⁶ s. Light travels at 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Use distance = speed × time to calculate how far the pulse travels in that time. Give your answer as an ordinary number.
practice.hint: Multiply the front numbers (3 × 2) and add the powers (8 + (−6)), then write the result out in full.

practice.question: Each electron carries a charge of 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. In one second 5 × 10¹⁹ electrons pass a point in a wire. Calculate the total charge that passes. Give your answer as an ordinary number.
practice.hint: Total charge = number of electrons × charge on one electron; multiply the front numbers and add the powers.

types.name: Rearranging an equation to find the unknown
types.method: Write the equation, list what you know, and circle the one quantity you do not. Undo whatever is being done to that quantity: a quantity that is multiplied is found by dividing, a quantity that is divided is found by multiplying, and a quantity that is squared is found by taking the square root last. Substitute only after rearranging, or substitute first and then solve, but keep the units with the numbers.
commonErrors: Dividing the wrong way round (I = V / P instead of I = P / V)
Forgetting to take the square root at the end when the unknown is squared
Taking the square root before dividing out the other quantities
Rearranging ρ = m / V to V = ρ / m instead of V = m / ρ

worked.question: A kettle has a power of 2300 W and is connected to the 230 V mains. Use P = I × V to calculate the current in the kettle.
steps: Known: P = 2300 W, V = 230 V. Unknown: I.
P = I × V → I = P / V
I = 10 A

practice.question: A sack of potatoes has a weight of 450 N. Use W = m × g to calculate its mass.
practice.hint: m is multiplied by g, so divide the weight by g = 10 N/kg.
walkthrough: W = 450 N, g = 10 N/kg, find m.
W = m × g → m = W / g

practice.question: Glass has a density of 2500 kg/m³. A glass block has a mass of 5 kg. Use ρ = m / V to calculate its volume.
practice.hint: V is on the bottom of the fraction: swap V and ρ so that V = m / ρ.
walkthrough: ρ = 2500 kg/m³, m = 5 kg, find V.
ρ = m / V → V = m / ρ

practice.question: A climber of mass 60 kg gains 3000 J of gravitational potential energy on a climbing wall. Use GPE = m × g × h to calculate the height climbed.
practice.hint: h is multiplied by both m and g, so divide the energy by m × g.
walkthrough: GPE = 3000 J, m = 60 kg, g = 10 N/kg, find h.
GPE = m × g × h → h = GPE / (m × g)

practice.question: A cyclist and bike of total mass 50 kg have 3600 J of kinetic energy. Use KE = ½ × m × v² to calculate the speed of the cyclist.
practice.hint: First find v² by doubling the energy and dividing by the mass; take the square root last.
walkthrough: KE = 3600 J, m = 50 kg, find v.
KE = ½ × m × v² → v² = 2 × KE / m

practice.question: A train accelerates at 2 m/s² over a distance of 200 m and reaches a velocity of 30 m/s. Use v² − u² = 2 × a × x to calculate its initial velocity.
practice.hint: Find u² first: u² = v² − 2 × a × x, then take the square root.
walkthrough: v = 30 m/s, a = 2 m/s², x = 200 m, find u.
v² − u² = 2 × a × x → u² = v² − 2 × a × x

practice.question: A spring with a spring constant of 50 N/m stores 1 J of elastic potential energy. Use E = ½ × k × x² to calculate its extension.
practice.hint: Find x² by doubling the energy and dividing by k, then take the square root.
walkthrough: E = 1 J, k = 50 N/m, find x.
E = ½ × k × x² → x² = 2 × E / k

types.name: Percentages and ratios in physics
equations: efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input
types.method: A percentage is a fraction of the whole multiplied by 100. Efficiency is the useful output divided by the total input; multiply by 100 to give it as a percentage. For a percentage change, divide the change by the original value, not the new one. A ratio of two quantities is one divided by the other and has no unit.
commonErrors: Dividing the input by the output and getting an efficiency over 100%
Dividing a percentage change by the new value instead of the original
Forgetting to multiply by 100 when a percentage is asked for
Using the wasted energy as the useful output

worked.question: An electric motor is supplied with 500 J of energy and does 350 J of useful work lifting a load. Calculate the efficiency of the motor as a percentage.
steps: Known: useful output = 350 J, total input = 500 J. Unknown: efficiency.
efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input
efficiency = 350 / 500 = 0.7
As a percentage: 0.7 × 100 = 70%

practice.question: A kettle is supplied with 360 000 J of energy and transfers 324 000 J to the water. Calculate the efficiency of the kettle as a percentage.
practice.hint: Useful output divided by total input, then × 100.
walkthrough: efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input

practice.question: A transformer has 400 turns on its primary coil and 50 turns on its secondary coil. Calculate the ratio of primary turns to secondary turns.
practice.hint: Divide the primary turns by the secondary turns; a ratio has no unit.

practice.question: A car's speed increases from 20 m/s to 25 m/s. Calculate the percentage increase in speed.
practice.hint: Find the change first, then divide by the original speed (20 m/s), not the new one.

practice.question: A litre of petrol stores 30 MJ of chemical energy. A car engine transfers 28% of this usefully. Calculate the useful energy transferred, in joules.
practice.hint: Change 30 MJ to joules first, then find 28% by multiplying by 0.28.

practice.question: An LED lamp has an input power of 12 W. It wastes 2.4 W as heat. Calculate the efficiency of the lamp as a percentage.
practice.hint: Find the useful power first by subtracting the wasted power from the input.
walkthrough: efficiency = useful power output / total power input

practice.question: A 0.5 kg ball is dropped from a height of 2.0 m and bounces back up to a height of 1.4 m. Calculate the percentage of its gravitational potential energy that is lost in the bounce.
practice.hint: Work out the GPE at each height with GPE = m × g × h, find the energy lost, then divide by the original GPE and × 100.
